Joanne Brackeen

Joanne Brackeen was born in Ventura, California on July 26, 1938. A self- taught jazz pianist, she worked in Los Angeles with Dexter Gordon and Charles Lloyd, and moved to New York in 1965. Joanne has recorded her original compositions with Art Blakey, Stan Getz and Joe Henderson and leads her own trio in performances here and abroad.
Joanne was interviewed in New York City on January 10, 2001, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming in New York City at the International Association of Jazz Educators. And I’m very pleased to have Joanne Brackeen here. And welcome and thank you very much for coming.
Oh you’re welcome.
I’d like to congratulate you on your career so far.
Thank you.
It’s an interesting read. And I’d like to venture kind of guess that your composing is just as important as your playing? Perhaps more so?

Well I don’t know about that. But it’s definitely very important, yeah. I mean a lot of my playing, the development of my playing I feel came out of learning how to play the compositions that I play, and the compositions very often come as spontaneously as improvising does. Parts. I mean I don’t just sit down and play and spontaneously that’s a composition, although that could happen. But I’ll edit and put this here or there. Whatever. But many times when I’m doing parts of a composition I’m playing some things that I’ve never played before and when I write them down and try to play them again I can’t do it.
Isn’t that interesting.
So you’re coming from another place which is very similar to the place that happens when I am improvising. So I would say they’re very, very connected.
Sometimes when you look at a piece of music rhythmically, written down, it does seem harder to play when you’re reading it than just in doing it.

Well I didn’t mean that, that’s definitely true in my case, but I didn’t mean just that. No even if you know what that is, it’s not like that, it’s like somebody else wrote this, how in the world could someone play this. And then in a week or whatever I’ve got it.
What kind of caught your ear when you were young, that led you down this path?

The sound of the piano. Simple as that. I love the sound of the piano. And it’s interesting too because when I hear the sound of the piano I love it, but I also hear a sound of an © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

orchestra inside the sound of the piano. So I wrote a string quartet, it was very easy for me to play the violin part. It’s like I’m already hearing that. So it’s something I didn’t really notice, but it was there from the beginning, I hear an orchestra there.
I read an interesting little tidbit, that someone said that one of your early influences was Frankie Carle?

Um hmm. Absolutely. Really that was how I learned how to play. I liked his solos. I liked his piano playing. And there was one album, I think it was called “Frankie Carle and his Girlfriends,” and so it was like Diane and Charmaine and Louise and I learned these solos note for note when I was eleven. I played them actually. I began performing them.
No kidding?

The whole solos, the whole thing, exactly what you heard on the record, that’s what I played. So after doing maybe six months of that, and maybe I did eight or ten of them, I knew how to play the piano.
When you were playing them, I’m trying to figure out how to say this, did you know what you were playing from a harmonic standpoint?

I just heard. I still, that’s how I go now, what I do now. People say “What’s that” and, “what’s that,” and I say well it’s the music, here it is, this is what it is. And I still don’t have a definite definition of everything.
Interesting. When you do a lead sheet on a new composition.
I try. I try.
You come as close as the chord language will allow?

Well sometimes it’s like a one chord over another chord, but the other chord has maybe it’s over the third of that chord, but you also have to have the tonic, the root of that in there too. So it’s like well you want the E flat but if you called it an E flat that would be on the bottom but it’s not. So then I’ve got three chords there. So there are different ways to notate it by the time I look at that I would never just spontaneously figure it out. So I do what I can.
Was Los Angeles — that’s where you’re from, correct?
Um hum. Actually born in Ventura.
Was it a good musical atmosphere to grow up in?
Well it had been. It was before I was there. And a little bit was still left. There was a lot of jazz there when I was too young to —
Central Avenue and that —

Yeah. There was a lot. But there was a little bit left by the time I was fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, and I got out to hear that. I heard Art Blakey, I heard Johnny Griffin, and of course I heard Coltrane and I heard a lot of things, McCoy Tyner. It wasn’t like New York. And I always had a feeling that I wanted to be in New York, since I was six years © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

old I was drawing — and I’ve never heard or seen anything — but I was drawing these apartment buildings with little mice sticking out of them for people, like a lot of people in every window. It was very funny.
Neat.
Yeah.
How did your parents feel about your — the direction you seemed to be embracing in music?

Well they didn’t seem to think too much about it until they started hearing me on the radio and then they began to get a bit proud about it, when their friends said, “Oh I heard your daughter on the radio.” They liked that.
And I read you played with quite a good list of tenor players early on.
Um hum.
Harold Land and that group.

Yeah, they were from California, Harold Land, Teddy Edwards, Charles Lloyd. Those are the people that you would recognize. There were other people who just kind of that lived in this area that you wouldn’t have heard of so much. Walter Benton was one of the major people there. Ray Graziano. There were other people but the people that we are speaking of are the ones that are kind of known all over.
Uh huh. So in order to play with these musicians, what kind of preparation did you undergo. Was it — did someone tell you to learn the standards and all that?
No. Nobody told me anything.
No kidding.

It was very weird. They didn’t have really schools that much. There was one school called the Westlake College of Music. And my parents took me there when I was fourteen and I remember studying a little bit with a piano player named Dave Robertson and also one named Gene Garf. And I remember Gene Garf liked Art Tatum a lot and I didn’t at that time. And they would give me a tune a week or something, I would learn a tune, and it would be a standard. They didn’t say anything and it really, there was no way that you learned scales and how to play on things, they just said here’s a tune, you know, improvise on it. So I did. It was kind of hard. But I learned how to do it. I don’t know how I did. And then of course I heard Charlie Parker and that did it for me when I heard that. You know whatever Art Tatum had done for the previous piano teacher, Charlie Parker did that for me. And then of course Bud Powell. So those were my favorites right when I was like seventeen, eighteen. And I used to transcribe the whole thing you know, so I could play it on the record, like a record like that over there, that’s what we had are 33s. And I’d put the record on, transcribe the Bird solo and the Bud solo, so I could play the whole thing. And it would be a half a tone sharp so if it was in the key of F it would © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

be G flat. But you know the funny thing about not knowing anything too much and not having many teachers was that I didn’t know that was hard, or I didn’t think too much, it was just something I really liked to do. And I thought that the feeling of the music was incredible. I still feel that way when I hear Bird and Bud. Nothing left. So those two are really amazing. A lot of times you hear music, of course I have a different opinion of Art Tatum, I love him now too. But sometimes you know you hear music and it seems to — it changes. It doesn’t but you change and so it sounds changed. But they didn’t.
Do you think Tatum was perhaps too technical for your ears at the time? Or can you think back on that?

I don’t know what it was. I kind of liked the rhythmical feeling of what Bird and Diz and many other people too, Tommy Flanagan was one of the first people I heard, Sonny Rollins, I just thought they were fantastic. I like the rhythmical essence there, and while Art Tatum had it, he would kind of venture off of it and I’m like, now why is he doing that? But then later on, as you get to know the piano better, he is totally amazing. And I love him. And I can listen to him any mood at any time.
Um hum. I like the statement you pointed out just a moment ago though about the not knowing something was supposed to be difficult.
Yes. No, there were no teachers then.
Right. So it didn’t get in your way, that you had to play in the key of G flat.
No, I didn’t know.
Very interesting. Was there a point where you said to yourself I’m going to make a career out of this?

Yes but it was much, much later than you would think. I’d been doing it for a very long time. I would say, let’s see, it was one year before people began to know who I was. 1968, I thought, you know I think I want to really do this. I didn’t really define what it was or who I wanted to do it with but that I think was already defined in what I heard and what I felt and the people who played in that kind of an essence. A strong, a kind of a really strong feeling.
Did you do non-musical work before, to make a living, before you kind of jumped into the music thing?
No I mean I was always a musician.
You were always a musician.
Yeah, yeah. I started when I was eleven, so I was working by the time I was twelve.
Can you remember what you made on your first paying gig?

No. I don’t. But well there was one that I do remember, because I remember being able to go out and buy a coat, a cashmere coat. This was so long ago, of what would be the — what it would be now I can’t imagine. I guess if you would times it by twenty, it would © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

be maybe about two thousand dollars a week now, what it was then. But that was when I was a teenager. I was still in high school and I was working six nights a week in this club. It was like a Latin club, it was called the Million Dollar Theater and we played Latin music. So that was fun. Six nights a week and then I had to try to get to school the next day.
Did your friends think that was pretty outrageous?
Most of them didn’t know.
Oh.
Only a few people knew. I didn’t tell everybody. Because that was another world that was busy, and then there was the school world.
Yeah. Were you anxious to get out of public school?

I didn’t really think school had much value for me after the age of ten or eleven. I had a few teachers that I did like, and I liked the way they taught, and that’s what intrigued — I wouldn’t care what the subject was, there were a few teachers, but not too many. Most of it I thought was kind of a waste of time.
So the pull of New York eventually got you I would imagine?
Yes. Well I was married then and my husband was from New York.
Charles?
And he wanted to come back, yeah. So we came back and we already had three children so we brought them back and then I had a fourth one here.
Was it culture shock?

No. No. It felt like that’s where I should have been from the beginning. Even though I love California, it’s beautiful, and being by the ocean, I have to be by the water. Even now you look out my apartment window and you see water. And I also have a beach house that reminds me of the place I was born. And it’s on the east coast but you know it’s kind of like I need both of those things: the busy, busy city and the very, very quiet by the ocean.
Do you think there is a west coast sound for jazz? You kind of always see that in the history books.

Well you know I mean the people that I heard probably because there was more west coast jazz. Friends introduced me to — I was talking to Chico Hamilton who teaches at the New School, telling him he was one of my first influences because it was Gerry Mulligan and Chet Baker and this is what I used to hear a lot of when I was say fifteen. I didn’t hear Bird until I was about seventeen, sixteen or seventeen. So yeah, I like that sound, and it did sound different. And Stan Getz was another one that I heard a lot of in California. So yeah, it did sound a lot different than the other thing, but I like them all. Every tune. I like a lot of different things. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
It’s interesting because some of those things early on seem to have come out in your playing and compositions, the Latin thing and—

Also I think, I don’t know what percentage, but I have some Spanish in me on my father’s side, so that I don’t know whether — well California has a lot of people who speak Spanish. They are not Spanish, they are more Mexican, but of course I had a lot of friends like that.
Was it difficult raising children in New York?

At the time you know we just made it. We just made it. There was a few schools left and you kind of had to give an address of a friend to get them in the right schools that were left. But just about the time they graduated I would say that it would be very difficult to raise them now, and school them the way that you want them schooled without a whole lot of money. It would have to be done privately. Things may change, but it was on the cusp. I had to move them from the school they should have gone to to one that was good. And they made it through.
What’s it like trying to — what year was this now? In the 60s you came here?
I came here in the 60s yeah.
To break in — well the 60s, maybe you can tell me as far as the decades for jazz, the 60s wasn’t one of the healthiest I don’t think.
Oh it was very innovative.
But as far as finding work, was it hard for you to find work here in New York?
Well I was working with Art Blakey so—
You couldn’t have done much better than that.

There was a lot of loft scenes around, and a lot of just sessions. People — I remember working in a club that didn’t pay anything but somehow I got hooked up with Pete LaRoca Sims and Dave Liebman and there was — if I could remember the name of the club, they’d know, La Boehme. We worked there six nights a week and Dave Holland used to come down. There was a lot of us that just — we would play, we would get paid something but not what you would consider very much. There was a lot of playing going on, innovative playing. People had their own signatures. They had their own, you know, everybody didn’t sound like one person, where we have a tendency now, that a lot of people tend toward that, not that that’s bad.

Do you think that, this is a point I was hoping to get to eventually so here we are, do you think that tendency for people to kind of sound like each other is because of the education that’s going on now or what is that about?

I’m not sure. I heard from historians that in art, there are certain periods that take place in finance, there are certain periods that take place, there’s periods where innovators are born and this goes out and moves in a certain way, and then after maybe eighty years or a © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

hundred and twenty years, whatever that cycle is, it seems to begin again. If you do a study, which I haven’t had the time but I do have the interest, in looking back at the cycles that’s hard to do though. Because our cycles now would be — the Internet and the computer are moving much differently. They are just speeded up so fast. I mean knowledge doubles every two or two and a half years, something like that. So it’s very exciting to be here now. But to answer that question, you know, there’s going to be another group. Life runs in cycles. And it’s nice to enjoy that cycle that we’re in. It’s quite amazing. But I’m glad that I was there in the cycle that I was in, there were a lot of what we call really innovators, people really seriously listening to their own voice. That comes first. The spiritual aspect, and naturistical too, coming first.
Jazz seems to move pretty fast in its development it seems like. Guys like Miles who just, when the audience catches up with him, he’s on to something else.
Um hum yeah. It works that way.
Yeah, I guess it does. How did the gig with Blakey come about?
Oh, that’s an interesting story. I lived right around the corner from this club called Slug’s.
Oh, Slug’s, I’ve heard this name, yes.

A tiny club. I mean it was bigger than this room, but not that much. It had sawdust all over the floor and you could get a beer for a dollar, and all the major groups were there. Art Blakey, Freddie Hubbard, McCoy Tyner, everybody, Lee Morgan. Everybody worked in there. And I lived right around the corner. So but I lived up like six flights of stairs, and I had four kids in five years, and they were very young, so I didn’t get out too often. So one night I heard that Art Blakey was there and I though oh I’ve got enough energy, I’m going to go around and see the band. So I’m saying this because I was kind of spaced out. It was late at night, and I also got up early in the morning. So I walked in there, and here was Art’s band. And they just sounded incredible. It was amazing music. And the piano player was sitting up there but he wasn’t playing. And it sounded like he should have been playing, it sounded like they needed the piano to play, you know, with the energy that they were playing in right there. So because I’m so spaced out, I’m just only hearing the music, I walked up to the bandstand and say, “Do you mind if I play?” And the piano player said, “No, go ahead.” It sounds funny but if you ever have four kids and you’re going six flights of stairs up and down for everything you’re doing during the whole day, by the time you get to the music it’s just, you’re so happy that you forget. And that’s what happened. And at the end of the set he looked up and saw me and I was hired. It was the furthest thing from my mind.
Oh, that’s fantastic. Who was in the band at that point?

I’m trying to remember. Carlos Garnett was in there. I haven’t heard him in a long time but I see he had a record out, I think it was last year, a new CD out. Actually the tour we © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

did Etta Jones was on but she wasn’t singing there. The bass player changed. It was Skip Crumby-Bey, but it changed to Jan Arnet, someone from Czechoslovakia that we only saw then. Of course we did go through several bass players and different people. And I think it was Randy Brecker, but he didn’t do some of the tours with us. We had Bill Hardman and we also had Woody Shaw, and other tenor players came in later, Ramon Morris, I think Buddy Terry did one job with him. So it was kind of a moving group.
He had a lot of energy, that band, didn’t he?
Yeah, he did. It was just like a jungle, it was great.
Did he encourage you to write for the band?

He was always telling me to write for the band but so was Stan Getz and I think that the only people that wanted to play my music were the rhythm sections. It was a long time before horn players came in and wanted to play. I think maybe one of the first was Mike Brecker. He’s on one of my first albums. He loved it. And then after that, now I have no problem. Not that everyone wants to do that but there is maybe five or six people that really — I’ve had Greg Osby do some things, Javon Jackson, Ravi Coltrane, Chris Potter was on one album, so, and there’s more, I don’t want to forget them but I can’t think of everyone at once. But in those days mainly the trios just wanted to play my music. So Stan tried a few times. Then what he did was actually feature the trio at the beginning of each set and we would play.
Now he was not a music reader, was he? He could read some?
He could read, I heard he didn’t but he could.
Okay. Maybe he preferred not to.
My tunes were a little bit more than what he wanted to get into.
Right. How is it different playing behind him than with Blakey? Did you feel—

Well it was two totally different things. I mean with Art Blakey you felt like you had a jungle power every time you played. It was incredible. With Stan it was much more sensitive. You had to really listen to every note. It was like playing with a singer. You know, you had to play all the right notes, all the right voicings, play just the time he wanted to hear, and he never said that but you could tell from the way he was playing. And with Stan I just got so very spoiled because he played so in pitch, you know his pitch was so perfect it really bothered me a long time afterward to play with anyone who wasn’t aware of — they could play out of the pitch but if they didn’t know, if they couldn’t play around with it and know where that center was, and I’m the same way with singers, so I became that way then with horn players.

That’s an interesting statement about playing behind singers. What do you tell, do you have advice for piano players when they are going to have to branch out into that kind of accompaniment scene? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Well I think now you just go tell them to buy ten CD’s of your favorite singer and listen to the piano player. Because that’s the best way to actually hear what the possibilities are. It’s much easier than the way we had to learn hit and miss.
Yeah.

But you have to hear everything, you don’t want to put something just before — every little hair matters, everything matters. It has to be relaxed and swinging too. It’s a lot of balance is going on and you just need to know that plus the harmonies and the lines. There’s a lot to it.
Have you had occasion where you’ve tried experimenting with maybe some substitutions and so forth with different singers, and you find that — not to do it.

Well I don’t really play with singers but you know the first thing that I always tell, and not everyone does this so you don’t have to do this, you know the way Herbie was playing behind Miles. Sometimes it sounds, he’s just got his rhythmic thing, and it’s so much fun, seemingly having nothing to do with Miles you know. So you could play that way too. He was hooking up a lot with the rhythm section and I’m sure that’s what Miles wanted at that time, if we’re thinking back into the mid-60s. But I always, when I’m playing behind someone I just hear what notes they’re going to use and what notes they’re not going to use, and I’m certainly not going to play things that are going to offend that. I’ll stretch it as far as I can go but not — to make it sound like one thing.
You’ve had pretty good success it seems with your recording career. Is it a challenge? Is it difficult to get records out and has it changed over the years?

Well I have a contract now so we’ve done four and we’re — I don’t know how many more we’ll do. It’s a long deal so probably there’ll be a lot more coming out. But if I look back over the ones as a leader that I’ve done I do on average one a year. Because I think I started in 1975, so there’s about 25 out. That’s the average. That’s the way it works out. There’s more than one some years, and—
Do you do your own business, I guess, pretty much?

Well I have a manager. You know I work with people and yeah, I get some help. Because you know when you’re touring it’s too hard, even with the — well I have to get a palm pilot, that’s what I think, so I can get the e-mail. I don’t have that yet. I just got a new computer. But even at that it’s a little difficult sometimes to keep up with things. You let too many things slide that you really want to do. So it’s good to have some people supporting you.
Is it somewhat easier now that your kids are grown?
Oh yeah. Of course, yes. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

I had a couple of things people have said about you. And Bill Dobbins at Eastman, he said your, “Approach to playing is unique especially in regards to rhythmic development.” Does that strike you as a good statement do you think?

I guess so. I mean that’s me. I would have to agree that he’s certainly — my students use so many of his transcriptions in learning things and learning how to play. There are some key things that he’s done, been a transcriber of, so he does a close study of people and things. So I highly regard him and respect him.

Good. This one is a little funny. It’s from the CD Guide to Jazz and it says, “Her chord voicings are quite dense but this music is strangely accessible.” Is that a left handed compliment? Isn’t that interesting.

Well I guess he probably just thought, I don’t know, it’s hard to make that out because you don’t know if he’s saying that the chords are dense in this or maybe they’re not dense in this. And also from about 1995 on up to now, 2001, the harmonies have worked in a lot more and also rhythms and time meters. There is a lot more going on in the music now than there was before, where you can so-called get away with almost anything you want to do. Not anything, but a lot. A lot more. It’s a lot more acceptable to play now like I did in 19— let’s see when I did that one for Columbia “Tappan Zee,” 1979, 1980, I go back and listen to those about once every five years, and that playing is what people are doing now. So it’s okay to do that now. So maybe that’s what’s happening. I don’t know what the phenomenon might be.

Playing, as you describe almost anything, if your students were playing something and you thought they had no basis for what they were doing, is there a point where you want them to at least have some grounding? I’m not asking this very well. I’m trying to think, playing outside, but still knowing what you’re outside from. Does that make any sense?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. They have to — sometimes usually if they do that it’s the rhythmical sense that isn’t developed that much. And so I bring them in and make sure that they can do that too. But I never stop them from doing what they’re doing. Because I think you can learn in many different realms, you know, points of view at one time. And if a person has started developing one thing, they’re very interested in that. So to stop that doesn’t make sense to me. So I let them keep on unless it’s something just totally disastrous. But that seldom happens. But what I’ll do is given them examples and show them how important, you know, usually I’ll do it through players. You’ve got so many players, recordings are so available, it’s easy to give references, and then they can understand.
Who are your musical — oh, pioneers for you, besides Frankie Carle?

Well he wasn’t really a pioneer. My parents had the record and that’s how I got that. But the first people like I think I mentioned before that I heard, it was like you know Bird and Bud and Miles and Tommy Flanagan, Arthur Taylor, Max Roach, some of my favorite © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
people. I guess I’m not naming bass players. They change so much. And then we had Paul Chambers later on. So I liked the piano and the sax and drums most, until I started like that.
You’ve had some marvelous bass players on your recordings over the years.

Yeah. Well when I was in Los Angeles we played, I mean Scott LaFaro was one of the bass players that I played with. Charlie Haden. They were from there. So that was right from the start so that was kind of my expectation was people like that.
Is it possible to keep a band together these days?

Well you know what you do, or what I do is, you kind of have multiple bands. You find people, maybe two or three people that are really into your music on each instrument. Because people are working in so many different groups and we travel so much, so it’s really great when you’ve got your key people there. But I try to have maybe two people on each instrument, maybe a third. Then if one’s not available, they kind of know the vocabulary. Because outside of that it wouldn’t work. I’m even going to Tel Aviv next week and I’m lucky because Ira Coleman has been working on and off with me for about ten years, and Dion Parsons is new but he’s a friend of Ira’s, so he’s been working with me for about a year. So it’s easy. We call one rehearsal. They already have a good idea of what we might do. And that way, you know, maybe there’s twenty-five tunes, maybe we’re only going to play fifteen but we can decide, and put something new in there. It’s difficult just to get a band and rehearse a set, this, this and, you know.
Do you find it different overseas as far as the audience for your music?

Well I haven’t had too many calls to do that music — no I can’t say that, I do do that. I worked at the Jazz Standard every year here and then I kind of work some subterranean clubs because I like to do that. So one club is, they get so many people in the club that they don’t advertise.
Is that right?

It’s fun, yeah. And I do that maybe two or three times a year, and then I worked in the main club, the Jazz Standard. We get great reception now. We get great reception also in Europe. So it’s hard to say. Sometimes in the European audiences, I mean you can tell they haven’t heard this kind of music, whereas in New York it’s a great audience, but they are a little more sophisticated — maybe less jumping up and down and like little kids in Europe. That’s great but I can’t say that one is more appreciative than the other. I think that there’s a lot of appreciation. The one thing that does seem to happen more in Europe is there are more venues per the population so the sense of culture and art is, and it’s a much older country, they developed more. But we have just great music here. I still prefer our music. You know, our musicians, our music. I was reading articles and hearing © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
people saying oh the music here is becoming like kind of backwards and it’s more creative in Europe. But I don’t join that. I’m kind of international. I see it all as one thing.
The term “world music” has entered kind of just as a phrase. And it’s amazing how fast things get spread around now with communication. And I like to think of our music as world music too.
Well it is. It is. I know those computers, they really do something.
Did I see you had a part in this “Hundred Fingers?”
Oh, Gold Fingers, yeah. Yeah ten piano players, we go to Japan every other year and they take what they call, what I heard, one token woman each time.
Is that right?
